segments.t: After seeing Sigourney Weaver with young actor Gaspard Ulliel, director Guillaume decides to switch the roles in his movie. However, when Sigourney joins him at a cafe, they learn that the distributor has abruptly pulled out. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait là-bas?
Elle s'achète une tour Eiffel?
J'ai changé d'avis pour le film.
Sigourney va jouer avec Gaspard Ulliel!
Le sujet, c'est l'amour, non?
Bonjour Guillaume! Comment allez-vous?
Bonjour Sigourney! Pas trop fatiguée?
Fatiguée? Pourquoi? Pas du tout!
Un espresso très serré, s'il vous plaît.
J'ai une mauvaise nouvelle, je suis désolé.
Le distributeur s'est retiré du projet.
Quoi? Il refuse d'inverser les rôles?
Laissez-moi aller me changer!
Sigourney, vraiment? Qu'allez-vous faire?
Let's examine the conversation line by line and explore the French expressions.
Qu'est-ce qu'elle fait là-bas?
'What is she doing over there?' Guillaume spots Sigourney standing on the footbridge. The clause hinges on the everyday verb meaning 'does'.
Elle s'achète une tour Eiffel?
'Is she buying herself an Eiffel Tower?' Guillaume is amused to see her shopping for trinkets. Notice how 'buys' leads directly into the noun meaning 'tower'.
J'ai changé d'avis pour le film.
'I changed my mind about the movie.' Guillaume tells Gabriel that he is revising the script. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past verb form for 'have'.
Sigourney va jouer avec Gaspard Ulliel!
'Sigourney will act with Gaspard Ulliel!' Guillaume pairs the American icon with the young French star. Dropping the subject pronoun turns the verb for 'is going to' into a direct, punchy command.
Le sujet, c'est l'amour, non?
'The subject is love, is it not?' Guillaume argues that romance transcends age differences. The key noun here means 'subject', anchored by its matching French article.
Bonjour Guillaume! Comment allez-vous?
'Hello Guillaume! How are you doing?' Sigourney arrives at the cafe table in high spirits. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past verb form for 'are you doing'.
Bonjour Sigourney! Pas trop fatiguée?
'Hello Sigourney! Not too tired?' Guillaume checks on his leading lady after her outing. The adjective meaning 'tired' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Fatiguée? Pourquoi? Pas du tout!
'Tired? Why? Not at all!' Sigourney brushes off any suggestion of fatigue. The adjective meaning 'tired' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
Un espresso très serré, s'il vous plaît.
'A very strong espresso, please.' Sigourney orders a concentrated coffee from the waiter. The key noun here means 'espresso', anchored by its matching French article.
J'ai une mauvaise nouvelle, je suis désolé.
'I have bad news, I am sorry.' Guillaume hangs up his phone with a worried look. The verb meaning 'have' pairs naturally with the noun for 'news' in everyday conversation.
Le distributeur s'est retiré du projet.
'The distributor pulled out of the project.' Guillaume explains that their financier backed out. Notice how 'has' leads directly into the noun meaning 'distributor'.
Quoi? Il refuse d'inverser les rôles?

'What? He refuses to switch the roles?' Sigourney realizes the distributor doubts an older leading woman. In everyday spoken French, rising intonation on 'refuses' at the end is enough to turn the sentence into a question.
Laissez-moi aller me changer!
'Let me go change my clothes!' Sigourney decides to confront the distributor in person. This conversational past tense combines a helper verb with the past verb form for 'let me'.
Sigourney, vraiment? Qu'allez-vous faire?

'Sigourney, really? What are you going to do?' Guillaume is astonished by her bold determination. Inverting the verb and pronoun around 'are you going to' creates a crisp, polished question. Now let's listen to the complete discussion once more to reinforce the vocabulary.

Refusing to let the film fall apart, Sigourney Weaver prepares to confront the distributor directly. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'does' and 'buys'. You'll catch them now. See you next time.
Bonne soirée!
